trick: Hardly...when is correct; suspect it only when paired with 'than'.

statement: Find the part of the sentence that has an error: (A) A number of students / (B) were absent / (C) because of the transport strike.
explanation: There is no error. 'A number of + plural noun' means 'many' and takes a plural verb, unlike 'The number of', which is singular.
trick: A number of = plural verb; the number of = singular verb.

statement: Find the part of the sentence that has an error: (A) The teacher explained the concept / (B) clearly, and every student / (C) understood it.
explanation: There is no error. The adverb 'clearly' correctly modifies 'explained', and both clauses are complete and correctly joined.
trick: Not every long sentence hides an error; verify each part.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'She don't know the answer.'
explanation: With he/she/it, the negative of 'do' is 'doesn't', and the main verb stays in its base form: 'doesn't know'. 'Doesn't knows' wrongly marks the verb twice.
trick: After does/doesn't, always use the base verb.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'I have seen him yesterday.'
explanation: The present perfect cannot be used with a finished time marker like 'yesterday'. A completed past action with a definite time takes the simple past: 'I saw him yesterday'.
trick: 'Yesterday/last night/ago' → simple past, never present perfect.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'The teacher gave us many advices.'
options: The teacher gave us many advices.
The teacher gave us much advices.
The teacher gave us a large number of advices.
The teacher gave us a lot of advice.
explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable and has no plural form 'advices'. It is quantified with expressions like 'a lot of' or 'much': 'a lot of advice'.
trick: Advice, information and furniture cannot be counted directly.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'He is senior than me.'
explanation: Adjectives of Latin origin such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take the preposition 'to', not 'than': 'senior to me'.
trick: Senior/junior/superior + to, never than.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'I am looking forward to meet you.'
options: I am looking forward to meeting you.
I am looking forward to meet you.
I am looking forward for meeting you.
I am looking forward to meets you.
explanation: In 'look forward to', the word 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so it is followed by a gerund: 'to meeting you'.
trick: Look forward to + -ing, because this 'to' is a preposition.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Neither of the answers are correct.'
options: Neither of the answers are correct.
Neither of the answers be correct.
Neither of the answers is correct.
Neither of the answers were correct.
explanation: 'Neither' means 'not one of two' and is singular, so it takes 'is'. The plural noun after 'of' does not control the verb.
trick: Neither/either/each + singular verb.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'The committee have submitted its report.'
options: The committee have submitted their report.
The committee have submitted its report.
The committee are submitted its report.
The committee has submitted its report.
explanation: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb and pronoun. The committee acts together here, so 'has submitted its report' is correct.
trick: When the group acts as one body, treat it as singular.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'She asked me where was I going.'
options: She asked me where I was going.
She asked me where was I going.
She asked me that where I was going.
She asked me where I am going.
explanation: In an indirect question, the word order becomes statement order (subject + verb) and the tense shifts back: 'where I was going'. Question inversion is used only in direct questions.
trick: Indirect questions: no inversion, no question mark.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Although he was tired, but he continued working.'
options: Although he was tired, he continued working.
Although he was tired, but he continued working.
Although he was tired, but still he continued working.
Although he was tired, yet but he continued working.
explanation: 'Although' and 'but' both join the same contrast, so using both is redundant. Standard English keeps only one: 'Although he was tired, he continued working'.
trick: Although pairs with a plain clause or 'yet', never with 'but'.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'The book is too interesting that I cannot stop reading it.'
options: The book is too interesting that I cannot stop reading it.
The book is very interesting that I cannot stop reading it.
The book is so interesting that I cannot stop reading it.
The book is such interesting that I cannot stop reading it.
explanation: 'Too' is used with 'to' (too + adjective + to), while result clauses with 'that' need 'so': 'so interesting that I cannot stop'. 'Such' would need a noun phrase.
trick: So + adjective + that; too + adjective + to.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'I prefer coffee than tea.'
options: I prefer coffee over than tea.
explanation: The verb 'prefer' compares with the preposition 'to', not 'than': 'prefer coffee to tea'. The same pattern applies to the noun 'preference for'.
trick: Prefer X to Y is a fixed pattern.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'He has been suffering from fever since three days.'
options: He has been suffering from fever since three days.
He has been suffering from fever from three days.
He has been suffering from fever since three days ago.
He has been suffering from fever for three days.
explanation: 'Since' is used with a point of time (since Monday), while 'for' is used with a duration (for three days). A period of three days therefore needs 'for'.
trick: For = duration; since = starting point.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'No sooner did the bell ring when the students rushed out.'
options: No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out.
No sooner did the bell ring when the students rushed out.
No sooner the bell rang than the students rushed out.
No sooner did the bell rang than the students rushed out.
explanation: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', and with the auxiliary 'did' the main verb stays in base form 'ring'. Both conditions are met only in the correct option.
trick: No sooner...than; did + base verb.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Each boy and each girl were given a prize.'
options: Each boy and each girl were given a prize.
Each boy and each girl have given a prize.
Each boy and each girl are given a prize.
Each boy and each girl was given a prize.
explanation: When two singular subjects are joined by 'and' but each is preceded by 'each' or 'every', the verb remains singular: 'was given'.
trick: Each/every before joined subjects → singular verb.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'The reason for his failure is because he did not study.'
options: The reason for his failure is because he did not study.
The reason for his failure is due to because he did not study.
The reason for his failure is that he did not study.
The reason for his failure is owing because he did not study.
explanation: 'The reason is because' is redundant because 'because' itself means 'the reason is'. The standard form is 'The reason... is that...'.
trick: Reason + that; never reason + because.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'She is one of the best players who has ever played.'
options: She is one of the best players who has ever played.
She is one of the best players who is ever played.
She is one of the best players which has ever played.
She is one of the best players who have ever played.
explanation: In 'one of the + plural noun + who', the relative pronoun refers to the plural noun 'players', so the verb is plural: 'players who have ever played'.
trick: Look past 'one of' to the plural noun before 'who'.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Let us discuss about the new plan.'
options: Let us discuss about the new plan.
Let us discuss on the new plan.
Let us discuss regarding on the new plan.
Let us discuss the new plan.
explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb that takes a direct object without a preposition: 'discuss the plan'. 'Discussion about' is used only with the noun form.
trick: Discuss + object; never discuss about.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'He returned back to his village.'
options: He returned back to his village.
He returned back to village of his.
He was returned back to his village.
explanation: 'Return' already means 'go back', so 'back' is redundant. The clean standard form is 'He returned to his village'.
trick: Delete 'back' after return, and 'again' after repeat.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Being a rainy day, we stayed indoors.'
options: Being a rainy day, we stayed indoors.
Being a rainy day, the indoors was stayed by us.
It being a rainy day, we stayed indoors.
A rainy day being, we stayed indoors.
explanation: The original has a dangling participle because 'we' cannot be 'a rainy day'. Giving the participle its own subject fixes it: 'It being a rainy day, we stayed indoors'.
trick: A participle phrase needs a subject it can truly describe.

statement: Choose the grammatically correct version of: 'Supposing if it rains, the match will be cancelled.'
options: Supposing if it rains, the match will be cancelled.
Supposing if it will rain, the match will be cancelled.
If it will rain, the match will be cancelled.
If it rains, the match will be cancelled.
explanation: 'Supposing' and 'if' both introduce a condition, so they cannot be used together. Keeping only 'if' with the simple present gives the correct first conditional.
trick: Use one condition marker: if OR supposing, not both.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: I ___ him at the station last night.
explanation: The time marker 'last night' points to a finished past action, which takes the simple past 'saw'. The present perfect is impossible with a definite past time.
trick: Finished time words like 'last night' need the simple past.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: The quality of these pens ___ very good.
explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'quality'; the phrase 'of these pens' is only a modifier. A singular subject takes 'is'.
trick: Ignore the nearest noun; agree with the head noun 'quality'.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: She is ___ honest officer.
explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the 'h' is silent, so it takes 'an'. Articles are chosen by sound, not by the written letter.
trick: Silent h → an: an honest, an hour.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He has been ill ___ Monday.
explanation: 'Since' is used with a point of time, and Monday is a point where the illness began. 'For' would need a duration such as 'three days'.
trick: Since + day/date; for + number of days.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: Between you and ___, this secret is safe.
explanation: The pronoun follows the preposition 'between', so it must be in the objective case: 'me'. 'I' is used only as a subject.
trick: After any preposition, choose the object form.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: ___ you work hard, you will not pass the test.
explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not' and gives the required negative condition: only if you do not work hard will you fail. 'If you work hard' would reverse the meaning.
trick: Check whether the sentence needs a negative condition.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: By the end of 2027, the engineers ___ the new bridge.
explanation: 'By the end of 2027' marks a deadline in the future, and an action finished before that point takes the future perfect: 'will have completed'.
trick: 'By + future time' is the classic future-perfect signal.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: A pair of shoes ___ lying under the bed.
explanation: The subject 'a pair' is singular even though 'shoes' is plural, so the verb is 'was'. The noun after 'of' does not control agreement.
trick: A pair of / a bunch of + plural noun still takes a singular verb.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: She is fond of ___ in the school choir.
explanation: Prepositions are followed by the gerund form of a verb. After 'fond of', the correct form is 'singing'.
trick: Preposition + verb → always the -ing form.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He asked me ___ the window before leaving.
explanation: The pattern 'ask someone to do something' uses a to-infinitive after the object: 'asked me to close'. The bare infinitive is used after 'let' or 'make', not 'ask'.
trick: Ask/tell/want + person + to + verb.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: The boy ___ won the first prize is my cousin.
explanation: The relative pronoun refers to a person and works as the subject of 'won', so 'who' is correct. 'Whom' is used for objects and 'which' for things.
trick: Person + subject of the clause → who.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: This is the ___ chapter in the whole book.
explanation: The definite article 'the' and the phrase 'in the whole book' signal the superlative degree. For a long adjective, the superlative is 'most interesting'.
trick: 'The + ___ + in/of all' almost always needs the superlative.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: She is deeply interested ___ classical music.
explanation: 'Interested' is always followed by the preposition 'in'. This is a fixed adjective-preposition combination: 'interested in something'.
trick: Memorise pairs: interested in, afraid of, good at.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: ___ honesty is the best policy.
explanation: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article. The proverb speaks of honesty in general, so no article is used before it.
trick: General truths and abstract ideas usually drop the article.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He is both intelligent ___ hardworking.
explanation: 'Both' is always paired with 'and' in a correlative conjunction: 'both intelligent and hardworking'. Pairings like either-or and neither-nor follow the same logic.
trick: Both → and; either → or; neither → nor.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: You ___ stop your vehicle when the traffic light is red.
explanation: A traffic rule states a strict obligation, which is expressed by 'must'. 'Might' and 'could' express only possibility, which is too weak for a rule.
trick: Rules and duties → must; guesses → might/could.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He hurt ___ while climbing the stairs.
explanation: When the subject and object are the same person, a reflexive pronoun is used. Since he hurt himself (not another man), 'himself' is required.
trick: Same person as subject and object → reflexive pronoun.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: She told me that she ___ busy the previous day.
explanation: In reported speech, the tense moves one step back after a past reporting verb: 'am/is busy' becomes 'was busy'. 'The previous day' confirms the past reference.
trick: Said/told + past reporting → shift the tense back.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: There is very ___ sugar in the jar, so please buy some.
explanation: 'Sugar' is uncountable, and the sense is 'almost none', so 'little' is correct. 'Few/a few' are used only with countable nouns, and 'many' needs a plural noun.
trick: Uncountable + almost none → little; countable → few.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: If you had studied regularly, you ___ the scholarship.
explanation: The 'if' clause uses 'had studied' (third conditional), which talks about an unreal past. Its result clause takes 'would have won'.
trick: Had + past participle in the if-clause → would have + participle.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: The express train arrived ___ 9 p.m. sharp.
explanation: Clock times take the preposition 'at': at 9 p.m. 'On' is for days and dates, and 'in' is for months, years and parts of the day.
trick: At + time; on + day; in + month/year.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He stayed at home ___ he was not feeling well.
explanation: The second clause gives the reason for staying home, so the reason conjunction 'because' fits. 'Although/despite' would need a contrast, and 'unless' a condition.
trick: Ask: does the clause give a reason, contrast or condition?

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: Ten kilometres ___ a long distance to walk in this heat.
explanation: A plural-looking measure (distance, money, time) treated as a single unit takes a singular verb. 'Ten kilometres' is one distance here, so 'is' is correct.
trick: Sums and distances as one unit → singular verb.

statement: Fill in the blank with the correct option: The pending work ought to ___ before the audit begins.
explanation: 'The work' cannot finish something itself; it must receive the action, so a passive infinitive is needed after 'ought to': 'be finished'.
trick: If the subject receives the action, choose 'be + past participle'.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: She returned the old novels and renewed her membership card at the desk. Q: Anita visited the public library on Saturday morning. R: She then browsed the shelves and selected three new novels. S: Before leaving, she noted the due date in her diary.
explanation: The paragraph opens with the visit (Q), then the work at the desk (P), then selecting new books (R), and ends with noting the due date before leaving (S). Only QPRS keeps this time order.
trick: Look for opening sentences that introduce the person and place.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: Regular reading improves vocabulary and concentration. Q: It also exposes readers to new ideas and different viewpoints. R: For these reasons, even twenty minutes of reading a day can be valuable. S: As their vocabulary grows, students usually express their own ideas more clearly.
explanation: P states the main benefit, S grows out of the vocabulary point, Q adds another benefit with 'also', and R concludes with 'For these reasons'. The order is PSQR.
trick: A sentence beginning 'For these reasons' almost always ends the paragraph.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: He inspected the brakes and checked the tyre pressure carefully. Q: Ravi planned to cycle to the nearby lake at dawn. R: After packing water and a small repair kit, he set off from home. S: He reached the lake just as the sun was rising.
explanation: The plan (Q) must come first, followed by checking the cycle (P), setting off (R) and finally reaching the lake (S). The sequence is QPRS.
trick: Preparation comes before departure, and arrival comes last.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: The collected water is then passed through a simple filter. Q: Many houses now harvest rainwater from their rooftops. R: This filtered water can be used for gardening and cleaning. S: Gutters channel the rain into underground storage tanks.
explanation: Q introduces harvesting, S explains how rain reaches the tanks, P filters the collected water, and R states the use of 'this filtered water'. The order is QSPR.
trick: Follow the process step by step: collect → store → filter → use.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: These physical gains are matched by better mood and restful sleep. Q: Regular physical activity keeps the heart and muscles strong. R: Therefore, a daily walk is a simple habit with wide benefits. S: It can also reduce the risk of several lifestyle diseases.
explanation: Q gives the first benefit, S adds another with 'also', P refers back to 'these physical gains', and R concludes with 'Therefore'. The order is QSPR.
trick: Pronouns and phrases like 'these gains' point back to earlier sentences.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: At the plant, workers sort the materials by type. Q: Residents separate plastic, paper and metal at home. R: Trucks collect the sorted waste from each neighbourhood. S: Useful items are then cleaned and processed for reuse.
explanation: Recycling begins at home (Q), the trucks collect the waste next (R), sorting happens at the plant (P), and processing for reuse (S) completes the chain: QRPS.
trick: In process paragraphs, start where the material starts.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: The team divided the work according to each member's strengths. Q: Our class was asked to prepare a model of a smart city. R: We first discussed the design and listed the materials needed. S: After two weeks of steady work, the model was ready for display.
explanation: Q states the task, R begins the planning ('We first...'), P divides the work, and S reports the finished model after two weeks: QRPS.
trick: Words like 'first' and time spans like 'after two weeks' fix the order.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: Seeds were sown in neat rows and watered lightly. Q: Meena cleared a small patch of land behind her house. R: Within a few weeks, green shoots appeared across the patch. S: She loosened the soil and mixed in some compost.
explanation: The patch is cleared first (Q), the soil is prepared next (S), seeds are sown after that (P), and shoots appear 'within a few weeks' (R): QSPR.
trick: Soil is prepared before sowing; results always come after the action.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: He solved one mock test every evening under timed conditions. Q: Nikhil prepared a study timetable six weeks before the examination. R: He used the results to identify and revise his weak topics. S: This routine steadily improved both his speed and accuracy.
explanation: Q sets up the preparation, P describes the daily practice, R uses the test results for revision, and S sums up the effect of 'this routine': QPRS.
trick: A summary sentence ('This routine improved...') belongs at the end.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: Students can replay a recorded lesson whenever they need revision. Q: Online classes make learning possible from almost anywhere. R: They also save the time spent travelling to an institute. S: However, learners must remain disciplined without a classroom routine.
explanation: Q introduces online classes, P gives one benefit, R adds another with 'also', and S closes with the contrast marked by 'However': QPRS.
trick: 'However' signals a closing contrast after the benefits are listed.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: Residents dug pits along the road on Sunday morning. Q: The housing society decided to plant fifty saplings this year. R: Each family adopted one sapling and promised to water it regularly. S: By evening, the once-bare stretch of road looked green and welcoming.
explanation: The decision (Q) precedes the digging (P), families adopt saplings after planting is under way (R), and 'By evening' (S) closes the day's work: QPRS.
trick: Time markers like 'By evening' usually mark the final sentence.

statement: Arrange the following sentences in a meaningful order. P: He reached the station an hour before the train's departure. Q: Arun booked his train ticket a month in advance. R: After finding his seat, he placed his bag under the berth. S: The journey began as the train slowly left the platform.
explanation: Booking (Q) happens a month earlier, reaching the station (P) comes next, settling into the seat (R) follows, and the train leaving (S) ends the sequence: QPRS.
trick: Arrange events by their natural timeline: book → arrive → board → depart.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'The chef cooked a delicious meal.'
options: A delicious meal is cooked by the chef.
A delicious meal was cooked by the chef.
A delicious meal has cooked by the chef.
A delicious meal was cooking by the chef.
explanation: The active sentence is in the simple past ('cooked'), so the passive keeps the same tense: 'was cooked'. The object 'a delicious meal' becomes the subject.
trick: Keep the tense unchanged; only the voice changes.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'The teacher is explaining the lesson.'
options: The lesson is explained by the teacher.
The lesson was being explained by the teacher.
The lesson is being explained by the teacher.
The lesson has been explained by the teacher.
explanation: The active verb is present continuous ('is explaining'), so the passive is 'is being explained'. Dropping 'being' would change it to the simple present.
trick: Present continuous passive = is/are + being + past participle.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'They will complete the project tomorrow.'
options: The project will be completed by them tomorrow.
The project will completed by them tomorrow.
The project would be completed by them tomorrow.
The project is completed by them tomorrow.
explanation: With the modal/future auxiliary 'will', the passive is formed as 'will be + past participle': 'will be completed'. The time expression stays unchanged.
trick: Will → will be + V3 in the passive.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'Someone stole my bicycle yesterday.'
options: My bicycle has been stolen yesterday.
My bicycle was being stolen yesterday.
explanation: The action is simple past, so the passive is 'was stolen'. 'Yesterday' rules out the present perfect, and no continuous form is needed for a completed theft.
trick: A finished time marker ('yesterday') blocks present-perfect options.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'The committee approved the proposal.'
options: The proposal is approved by the committee.
The proposal was approved by the committee.
The proposal has approved by the committee.
The proposal approved by the committee.
explanation: 'Approved' is simple past, so its passive is 'was approved'. The subject of the passive sentence is the original object, 'the proposal'.
trick: Object becomes subject; verb becomes was/were + V3 for past tense.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'She can solve this problem easily.'
options: This problem can solved by her easily.
This problem could be solved by her easily.
This problem can be solved by her easily.
This problem is can be solved by her easily.
explanation: After a modal like 'can', the passive uses 'be + past participle': 'can be solved'. 'Could' would wrongly change the modal and the meaning.
trick: Modal + be + V3; never modal + V3 directly.

statement: Choose the correct active voice form of: 'The report was written by the manager.'
options: The manager has wrote the report.
The manager was written the report.
The manager is writing the report yesterday.
explanation: The passive 'was written' is simple past, so the active form uses the simple past 'wrote' with 'the manager' as the subject: 'The manager wrote the report'.
trick: In the active voice, the 'by' agent becomes the subject.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'The students have submitted their assignments.'
options: Their assignments are submitted by the students.
Their assignments were submitted by the students.
Their assignments has been submitted by the students.
Their assignments have been submitted by the students.
explanation: The active verb is present perfect ('have submitted'), so the passive is 'have been submitted'. The plural subject 'assignments' keeps 'have'.
trick: Present perfect passive = has/have + been + V3.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'He is watching an interesting movie.'
options: An interesting movie is watched by him.
An interesting movie is being watched by him.
An interesting movie was being watched by him.
An interesting movie has being watched by him.
explanation: A present continuous action ('is watching') becomes 'is being watched' in the passive. The other options change the tense or use a wrong form of 'be'.
trick: Continuous actions keep 'being' in the passive.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'The police arrested the thief last night.'
options: The thief is arrested by the police last night.
The thief has been arrested by the police last night.
The thief was arrested by the police last night.
The thief arrested by the police last night.
explanation: The simple past 'arrested' converts to 'was arrested'. 'Last night' confirms a finished past time, ruling out the present-tense and present-perfect options.
trick: Match both tense and time expression when changing voice.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'Finish the work at once.'
options: Let the work be finished at once.
The work is to finished at once.
You are finished the work at once.
The work at once be finish.
explanation: Imperative sentences form the passive with 'Let + object + be + past participle': 'Let the work be finished at once'. This keeps the command force of the original.
trick: Passive of an order: Let + object + be + V3.

statement: Choose the correct passive voice form of: 'Who wrote this poem?'
options: This poem was written by who?
By whom this poem was written?
By whom was this poem written?
explanation: When the question word is the object of a preposition in the passive, it becomes 'By whom', and the question keeps auxiliary inversion: 'By whom was this poem written?'
trick: In formal passive questions, 'who' after 'by' becomes 'whom'.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: She took part ___ the inter-college debate.
explanation: The fixed phrase is 'take part in', meaning to participate in an event. The other prepositions do not form this phrasal expression.
trick: Take part in = participate; learn it as one chunk.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: The outdoor match was put ___ because of heavy rain.
explanation: 'Put off' means to postpone, which fits a match delayed by rain. 'Put out' means extinguish and 'put up' means display or accommodate.
trick: Rain or delay in the sentence usually signals 'put off' = postpone.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: He has been suffering ___ a high fever since Monday.
explanation: The standard collocation is 'suffer from' an illness or problem. 'Suffering with' is a common learner error in this pattern.
trick: Suffer from fever/disease/loss — fix the pair in memory.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: The principal was pleased ___ the students' performance.
explanation: 'Pleased with' is the correct adjective-preposition combination for satisfaction with a thing or result. 'Pleased about' is used for events, not this object pattern in standard tests.
trick: Pleased with a thing/result; pleased at/about an event.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: If you do not know a word, look it ___ in a good dictionary.
explanation: 'Look up' means to search for information in a reference book or database. 'Look into' means investigate a matter, not search a word.
trick: Words and information are 'looked up'; matters are 'looked into'.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: At the reunion, I ran ___ an old school friend after many years.
explanation: 'Run into' someone means to meet them unexpectedly, which suits a reunion meeting after years. 'Run after' means chase and 'run over' means knock down.
trick: Unexpected meeting → run into (or bump into).

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: The committee turned ___ our proposal because of the high cost.
explanation: 'Turn down' means to reject, which matches the reason given (high cost). 'Turn up' means arrive or increase, and 'turn off' means switch off.
trick: A proposal or request that is rejected is 'turned down'.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: His excuse was so weak that it simply did not hold ___.
explanation: 'Hold water' is an idiom meaning to stand up to examination or seem true. A weak excuse 'does not hold water', i.e., it is not believable.
trick: Arguments and excuses 'hold water' when they are sound.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: With his fear of public speaking, he is not cut ___ for a career in sales.
explanation: The idiom 'cut out for' means naturally suited for a job or activity. He is 'not cut out for' sales because the job demands public confidence.
trick: Cut out for = suited for; usually used in negatives and questions.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: The peace talks broke ___ after both sides refused to compromise.
explanation: 'Break down' describes talks or negotiations failing or collapsing. 'Break out' is used for wars, fires or diseases beginning suddenly.
trick: Negotiations break down; wars and fires break out.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: I cannot put ___ with such rude behaviour any longer.
explanation: The phrasal verb 'put up with' means to tolerate. The 'with' already present in the sentence confirms this three-word pattern.
trick: Put up with = tolerate; the final 'with' is the giveaway.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: After his illness, the doctor advised him to give ___ smoking.
explanation: 'Give up' means to stop doing a habit, which fits the doctor's advice about smoking. 'Give away' means distribute and 'give in' means yield.
trick: Quitting a habit → give up.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: She made ___ a funny story to explain why she was late.
explanation: 'Make up' a story means to invent it. 'Make out' means to see or understand with difficulty, which does not fit inventing an excuse.
trick: Invented stories are 'made up'; so is a made-up excuse.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: The new traffic rules will come ___ force from next month.
explanation: The fixed expression is 'come into force', used when a law or rule starts to apply. None of the other prepositions forms this phrase.
trick: Laws and rules come into force on a fixed date.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: After years of dispute, the two brothers decided to bury the ___ and work together.
explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' is an idiom meaning to end a quarrel and make peace. The context of ending a long dispute confirms this expression.
trick: To make peace after a fight = bury the hatchet.

statement: Complete the sentence with the correct option: With her curly hair and smile, the child takes ___ her mother.
explanation: 'Take after' someone means to resemble an older relative in appearance or character. The resemblance to her mother makes 'after' correct.
trick: Take after = look or behave like a parent/relative.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: He said, “I am busy today.”
options: He said that he is busy today.
He said that he was busy that day.
He said that I was busy that day.
He told that he had busy that day.
explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'am' shifts to 'was', 'I' changes to 'he', and 'today' becomes 'that day': 'He said that he was busy that day'.
trick: Change tense, pronoun and time word — all three.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: She said to me, “I will help you tomorrow.”
options: She told me that she will help me tomorrow.
She told me that I would help her the next day.
She told me that she would help me the next day.
She told to me that she would help you tomorrow.
explanation: 'Said to me' becomes 'told me', 'will' becomes 'would', 'I' becomes 'she', 'you' becomes 'me', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. Only this option makes all the changes.
trick: Make a checklist: verb, pronoun, time expression.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: Ravi said, “I have completed my work.”
options: Ravi said that he had completed his work.
Ravi said that he has completed his work.
Ravi said that I had completed my work.
Ravi said that he completed his work yesterday.
explanation: The present perfect 'have completed' shifts to the past perfect 'had completed' in reported speech, and 'my' becomes 'his' for Ravi.
trick: Present perfect → past perfect after a past reporting verb.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: The teacher said to the students, “Open your books.”
options: The teacher asked the students that open your books.
The teacher told the students to opened their books.
The teacher said the students open their books.
The teacher instructed the students to open their books.
explanation: An imperative is reported with a reporting verb like 'instructed/ordered' followed by object + to-infinitive: 'instructed the students to open their books'.
trick: Commands: reporting verb + object + to + base verb.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: He asked me, “Where do you live?”
options: He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where I lived.
He asked me that where I live.
He asked me where you lived.
explanation: A reported Wh-question uses statement word order without inversion and shifts the tense back: 'where I lived'. No 'that' is placed before the question word.
trick: Indirect questions: subject before verb, no 'do/did' helping verb.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: She asked him, “Did you see the film?”
options: She asked him that did he see the film.
She asked him if he sees the film.
She asked him whether he had seen the film.
She asked him if you had seen the film.
explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', the simple past 'did see' shifts to the past perfect 'had seen', and 'you' becomes 'he'.
trick: Yes/no questions need if/whether in reported speech.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: She said to him, “Please help me with this bag.”
options: She requested him to help her with that bag.
She requested him that please help her with this bag.
She requested him to helps her with that bag.
She said to him politely to helping her with that bag.
explanation: A polite request with 'please' is reported as 'requested + object + to-infinitive': 'requested him to help her', with 'me' changing to 'her' and 'this' to 'that'.
trick: 'Please' in direct speech signals 'requested' in indirect speech.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: The captain said, “Hurrah! We have won the match.”
options: The captain said hurrah that we have won the match.
The captain exclaimed that hurrah, they won the match.
The captain happily said that we had won the match.
The captain exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
explanation: An exclamation of joy is reported with 'exclaimed with joy', 'we' becomes 'they', and 'have won' shifts to 'had won'. This option makes all three changes correctly.
trick: Match the reporting verb to the emotion: joy, sorrow, surprise.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: He said to her, “Will you come with me?”
options: He asked her will she come with him.
He asked her if she would come with him.
He asked her that she would come with me.
He asked her whether she will come with me.
explanation: A yes/no question uses 'if/whether', 'will' becomes 'would', 'you' becomes 'she', and 'me' becomes 'him' from the reporter's viewpoint.
trick: Track every pronoun from the new speaker's viewpoint.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: She said, “What a beautiful garden it is!”
options: She exclaimed that what a beautiful garden it was.
She said that it is a very beautiful garden.
She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful garden.
She asked what a beautiful garden it is.
explanation: An exclamatory sentence becomes a statement in reported speech: 'exclaimed that it was a very beautiful garden', with 'what a' replaced by 'very' and 'is' shifted to 'was'.
trick: Exclamations turn into plain statements with 'very/really'.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: The doctor said to the patient, “Take this medicine twice a day.”
options: The doctor advised the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor advised the patient that take this medicine twice a day.
The doctor told the patient to took this medicine twice a day.
The doctor asked the patient take that medicine twice a day.
explanation: Medical instructions are reported with 'advised + object + to-infinitive': 'advised the patient to take that medicine', with 'this' changing to 'that'.
trick: Advice from an expert → advised + object + to + verb.

statement: Choose the correct indirect speech form of: He said, “Let us go for a walk.”
options: He said that let us go for a walk.
He proposed that they would go for a walk.
He proposed that they should go for a walk.
He told that we should go for a walk.
explanation: A suggestion beginning with 'Let us' is reported with 'proposed/suggested that they should...'. The pronoun changes to 'they' and 'should' keeps the suggestion force.
trick: 'Let us' in direct speech → proposed that...should.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
explanation: Candid means frank and honest in speech; a candid person openly says what he or she truly thinks.
trick: Think of a candid photograph — unposed and natural, hence honest and direct.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to MITIGATE.
explanation: Mitigate means to make something less severe or serious; alleviate (to reduce suffering or severity) is its closest synonym.
trick: From Latin 'mitis' meaning mild — mitigate makes a problem milder.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to SCRUTINIZE.
explanation: Scrutinize means to examine something very carefully and in detail, looking for information or errors.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to DILIGENT.
explanation: Diligent means hardworking and careful about one's duties; industrious carries exactly the same meaning.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to AMBIGUOUS.
explanation: Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation, so it is unclear or vague in meaning.
trick: 'Ambi' means both — an ambiguous statement can be read both ways.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to CONCISE.
explanation: Concise means expressing much information in few words; a concise answer is brief and clear.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to HESITANT.
explanation: Hesitant means unsure or slow to act or speak; reluctant (unwilling and slow to act) is closest in meaning.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to APATHY.
explanation: Apathy is a complete lack of interest, enthusiasm or feeling about something — in other words, indifference.
trick: Greek 'a-pathos' means without feeling; apathy is having no feeling about a matter.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to VIVID.
explanation: Vivid means producing powerful and clear images in the mind; a vivid description is striking and easy to picture.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to INEVITABLE.
explanation: Inevitable means certain to happen and impossible to avoid, so unavoidable is the closest synonym.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to ENHANCE.
explanation: To enhance means to improve the quality, value or extent of something; improve is its direct synonym.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to SCARCE.
explanation: Scarce means present in a very small quantity, insufficient to meet the demand for it.
trick: Scarce is the opposite of abundant — eliminate 'plentiful' and 'common' first.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to TRANSPARENT, as used in the phrase 'a transparent explanation'.
explanation: In this context transparent means easy to understand and open — obvious; it does not carry the literal sense of being see-through here.
trick: Watch the context: transparent can mean see-through OR easy to understand.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to HOSTILE.
explanation: Hostile means unfriendly and opposed to something or someone; unfriendly is the closest synonym.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBSOLETE.
explanation: Obsolete means no longer used or produced because it has been replaced by something newer — outdated.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to METICULOUS.
explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to every detail; a meticulous worker is very careful and precise.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to INTRICATE.
explanation: Intricate means very complicated or detailed, with many small interconnected parts, like an intricate design.
trick: Picture an intricate pattern — many fine details woven together.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to VERIFY.
explanation: To verify means to check or test something in order to confirm that it is true or accurate.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABANDON.
explanation: To abandon means to give something up completely and leave it behind, for example abandoning a plan or a place.

statement: Choose the word closest in meaning to CRUCIAL.
explanation: Crucial means extremely important, because a final decision or result depends on it.
trick: From 'cross' — a crucial point is the crossing point where everything is decided.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ANCIENT.
explanation: Ancient means very old or belonging to the distant past; modern, meaning of the present time, is its direct opposite.
trick: 'Old' and 'antique' are synonyms, not opposites — eliminate them first.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to EXPAND.
explanation: Expand means to become or make larger; contract means to become smaller, which is the direct opposite.
trick: Extend, enlarge and spread all mean the same as expand — the odd one out is the answer.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
explanation: A transparent material allows light to pass through it; an opaque material does not allow light through at all.
trick: In the physical sense, transparent and opaque are a standard opposite pair.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to SCARCE.
explanation: Scarce means present in very small quantity; abundant means present in very large quantity, the exact opposite.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to HOSTILE.
explanation: Hostile means unfriendly and opposed; friendly is its direct opposite in meaning.
trick: Three options here are near-synonyms of hostile — pick the one that breaks the pattern.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to VICTORY.
explanation: Victory means winning a contest or battle; defeat means losing it, so the two words are direct opposites.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to INCLUDE.
explanation: To include means to make something part of a whole; to exclude means to deliberately leave it out.
trick: The prefix 'ex-' means out — exclude keeps something out.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to COURAGE.
explanation: Courage is the ability to face danger without fear; cowardice is the lack of courage and the tendency to run from danger.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TEMPORARY.
explanation: Temporary means lasting for only a limited time; permanent means lasting forever or for a very long time.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to GENUINE.
explanation: Genuine means truly what it is said to be; counterfeit means made in exact imitation of something valuable in order to deceive — a fake.
trick: Real, authentic and original are synonyms of genuine; counterfeit is the only fake-related word.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to MINIMUM.
explanation: Minimum is the smallest amount possible; maximum is the largest amount possible, its direct opposite.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ENCOURAGE.
explanation: To encourage means to give someone support and confidence; to discourage means to take away someone's confidence or enthusiasm.
trick: The prefix 'dis-' reverses the meaning, just as in agree/disagree.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to HUMBLE.
explanation: A humble person does not think too highly of himself; an arrogant person thinks he is better and more important than others.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to CHAOS.
explanation: Chaos means complete disorder and confusion; order, meaning a state of arrangement and organisation, is its opposite.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to FLEXIBLE.
explanation: Flexible means able to bend or change easily; rigid means stiff and unable to bend or change, the direct opposite.
trick: Bendable and adaptable are synonyms of flexible — eliminate them first.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to CONCEAL.
explanation: To conceal means to keep something hidden or secret; to reveal means to make it known or visible, the exact opposite action.
trick: Hide and cover are synonyms of conceal, so the answer must be reveal.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ADMIT.
explanation: To admit means to accept that something is true, often unwillingly; to deny means to state that something is not true.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to BROAD.
explanation: Broad means wide from side to side; narrow means small in width, which is the direct opposite.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to SHALLOW.
explanation: Shallow water has only a short distance from the surface to the bottom; deep water has a great distance, the opposite.
trick: 'Superficial' is a synonym of shallow in the figurative sense — watch out for it.

statement: Choose the word opposite in meaning to PROSPERITY.
explanation: Prosperity means the state of being wealthy and successful; poverty, the state of being extremely poor, is its direct opposite.
trick: Wealth, success and fortune are all companions of prosperity — only poverty opposes it.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who does not eat meat or fish.
explanation: A vegetarian is a person who does not eat meat or fish; a herbivore is an animal that eats only plants.
trick: A vegan avoids all animal products including milk and eggs — a stricter category than vegetarian.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: The scientific study of living organisms.
explanation: Biology is the science of living organisms; botany covers only plants, zoology only animals, and geology the earth.
trick: 'Bio' means life — any science of life in general is biology.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who is travelling on foot, rather than in a vehicle.
explanation: A pedestrian is a person walking on foot, especially along a road or in a city.
trick: 'Ped' relates to the foot, as in pedal — a pedestrian walks.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who does not believe in the existence of God.
explanation: An atheist is a person who disbelieves or lacks belief in the existence of God; a theist believes in God.
trick: The prefix 'a-' means without — an atheist is without belief in God.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who always looks at the bright side of things.
explanation: An optimist expects good things to happen and looks at the bright side; a pessimist expects the worst.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A government run by the people, usually through elected representatives.
explanation: Democracy is government by the people, exercised through elected representatives; a monarchy is ruled by a king or queen.
trick: 'Demo' means people and 'cracy' means rule — rule by the people.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who speaks many languages.
explanation: A polyglot is a person who knows or uses several languages; a linguist studies language scientifically, and a bilingual person speaks two.
trick: 'Poly' means many — many tongues make a polyglot; this is a classic placement-exam trap against 'linguist'.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who can use both hands equally well.
explanation: An ambidextrous person can use the right and left hands equally well; versatile means able to do many different things.
trick: 'Ambi' means both and 'dexter' means right/skilful — as if both hands were right hands.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A speech delivered without any previous preparation.
explanation: An extempore speech is spoken without preparation or notes; a lecture is a prepared educational talk.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A large enclosure where birds are kept.
explanation: An aviary is a large cage or enclosure for keeping birds; an apiary keeps bees and an aquarium keeps fish.
trick: 'Avi' relates to birds, as in aviation and avian — an aviary houses birds.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A person who loves mankind and works for its welfare.
explanation: A philanthropist promotes the welfare of others through generous donations and good works; a misanthrope dislikes mankind.
trick: 'Phil' means love — a philanthropist loves people, a philosopher loves wisdom.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A book or document written by hand.
explanation: A manuscript is an author's handwritten or typed text before it is printed and published as a book.
trick: 'Manu' means hand and 'script' means writing — hand-written text.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: A published collection of poems or other pieces of writing.
explanation: An anthology is a published collection of poems or other literary pieces by different or the same authors.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: Government by the wealthy.
explanation: Plutocracy is government or rule by the wealthy; aristocracy is rule by the nobility and bureaucracy rule by officials.
trick: From Greek 'ploutos' meaning wealth — follow the money in the word itself.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: The killing of one's own brother.
explanation: Fratricide is the act of killing one's own brother; patricide is killing one's father and homicide is killing a human being in general.
trick: 'Frater' means brother in Latin — all '-cide' words follow the pattern of who is killed.

statement: Choose the one word that best fits: One who has unlimited power.
explanation: Omnipotent means having unlimited power; omniscient means all-knowing and omnipresent means present everywhere at the same time.
trick: 'Potent' means powerful — omni + potent is all-powerful; do not confuse with omni-scient (all-knowing).

statement: In the sentence 'The coding test turned out to be a piece of cake for Ravi', the idiom 'a piece of cake' means:
explanation: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means something that is very easy to do, just as the test was easy for Ravi.

statement: In the sentence 'My manager calls a team lunch once in a blue moon', the idiom 'once in a blue moon' means:
explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely, because a blue moon itself is an uncommon event.

statement: In the sentence 'Sana did not attend the meeting as she was feeling under the weather', the idiom 'under the weather' means:
explanation: 'Under the weather' means feeling slightly ill or unwell, which is why Sana skipped the meeting.

statement: In the sentence 'To break the ice, the trainer began the session with a short game', the idiom 'break the ice' means:
options: To start a conversation in a social setting
explanation: 'Break the ice' means to do or say something that relieves initial shyness and gets people talking socially.

statement: In the sentence 'The developers burnt the midnight oil to release the app on time', the idiom 'burn the midnight oil' means:
options: Work or study late into the night
explanation: 'Burn the midnight oil' means to work or study late into the night, from the days when oil lamps were used after dark.

statement: In the sentence 'Karan spilled the beans about the surprise farewell party', the idiom 'spilled the beans' means:
explanation: 'Spill the beans' means to reveal secret information, usually unintentionally or before the right time.

statement: In the sentence 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise, as it pushed Meera to start her own company', the idiom 'a blessing in disguise' means:
options: A hidden benefit in something that first seemed bad
explanation: A 'blessing in disguise' is a good thing that first appeared to be bad or unlucky, exactly as losing the job later proved useful.

statement: In the sentence 'When you said the team needed clearer goals, you hit the nail on the head', the idiom 'hit the nail on the head' means:
explanation: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem — to say the precisely right thing.

statement: In the sentence 'The new laptop cost an arm and a leg, but it was worth it', the idiom 'cost an arm and a leg' means:
explanation: Something that 'costs an arm and a leg' is extremely expensive, as the costly laptop in the sentence.

statement: In the sentence 'Nobody was supposed to know, but Rohan let the cat out of the bag about the merger', the idiom 'let the cat out of the bag' means:
explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret, usually by accident or carelessness.

statement: In the sentence 'Stop beating around the bush and tell me the real reason for the delay', the idiom 'beating around the bush' means:
options: Avoiding saying what one really means
explanation: 'Beat around the bush' means to talk about unimportant things and avoid coming to the main point or saying what one means.

statement: In the sentence 'The accountant landed in hot water after the audit found missing bills', the idiom 'in hot water' means:
explanation: To be 'in hot water' means to be in a difficult situation or in trouble with someone in authority.

statement: In the sentence 'The two friends supported each other through thick and thin', the idiom 'through thick and thin' means:
options: In all circumstances, good and bad
With a great deal of effort
explanation: 'Through thick and thin' means through all circumstances, both favourable and unfavourable, without giving up.

statement: In the sentence 'Priya decided to bite the bullet and apologise to her team', the idiom 'bite the bullet' means:
options: Face an unpleasant situation with courage
explanation: 'Bite the bullet' means to force yourself to do something unpleasant or difficult that you have been avoiding.

statement: In the sentence 'I have given you all the details; now the ball is in your court', the idiom 'the ball is in your court' means:
options: It is now your turn to take action
explanation: From tennis, 'the ball is in your court' means it is now the other person's turn to act or make a decision.

statement: In the sentence 'To meet the deadline, the team cut corners while testing the product', the idiom 'cut corners' means:
options: Did something badly or carelessly to save time or money
explanation: 'Cut corners' means to do something in the easiest or cheapest way, sacrificing quality — here, testing was done carelessly.

statement: In the sentence 'Chasing that old rumour turned out to be a wild goose chase', the idiom 'a wild goose chase' means:
explanation: A 'wild goose chase' is a foolish, useless search for something that cannot be found or achieved.

statement: In the sentence 'The police realised they were barking up the wrong tree when the suspect produced his train ticket', the idiom 'barking up the wrong tree' means:
options: Following a wrong line of thought or accusing the wrong person
explanation: 'Barking up the wrong tree' means pursuing a mistaken line of thought or blaming the wrong person, as the police did here.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'to keep apart or divide into parts'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'separate' — remember there is 'a rat' in the middle: sep-A-RAT-e, a very common placement-exam word.
trick: There is 'a rat' in separate — use it to never misspell this word again.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'without any doubt; certainly'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'definitely' — it is built from the word 'finite' with the prefix de- and the suffix -ly.
trick: Find 'finite' inside definitely: de-FINITE-ly.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'an incident or event; something that happens'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'occurrence' — both the 'c' and the 'r' are doubled, because the stress falls on the second syllable of occur.
trick: Double c AND double r: o-CC-u-RR-ence.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'to make someone feel shy, ashamed or uncomfortable'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'embarrass' — it has double 'r' and double 's', a pair of doubles that many candidates miss.
trick: Double r, double s — embarrass has two of each.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'to provide space, lodging or a favour for someone'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'accommodate' — double 'c' and double 'm' both appear in this long word.
trick: Accommodate is roomy enough to hold two c's and two m's.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'the process of keeping something in good condition'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'maintenance' — note that the ending is -tenance, not -tainance, even though the verb is 'maintain'.
trick: Unlike 'maintain', the noun drops the second 'i': main-TEN-ance.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'the inner sense of what is right and wrong'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'conscience' — it contains the word 'science' after the prefix con-, which makes the -science ending easy to recall.
trick: Conscience = con + science.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'sometimes, but not often'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'occasionally' — double 'c', double 'l', and a single 's' in the middle.
trick: Double c, single s, double l — the pattern of occasional + ly.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'a set of written questions used to collect information'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'questionnaire' — borrowed from French, it keeps the double 'n' and ends with -aire.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'a period of one thousand years'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'millennium' — double 'l' and double 'n', since it comes from Latin 'mille' (thousand) and 'annus' (year).
trick: Double l for mille (1000) and double n for annus (year).

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'continued effort and determination despite difficulties'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'perseverance' — the middle portion is -sever-, from the word 'persevere', with an 'a' in -ance at the end.
trick: Build it from persevere + ance, keeping the 'a' of -ance.

statement: Choose the correctly spelt word meaning 'a regular pattern of beats or sounds in music or poetry'.
explanation: The correct spelling is 'rhythm' — a tricky word because it has no a, e, i, o or u; 'y' does the work of the vowel.
trick: Rhythm has no true vowel — remember its letters: R-H-Y-T-H-M.

statement: PEN : WRITE :: KNIFE : ?
explanation: A pen is used to write, and a knife is used to cut — the relation is tool to its main function.

statement: DOG : PUPPY :: CAT : ?
explanation: A puppy is a young dog, and a kitten is a young cat — the relation is animal to its young one.

statement: FISH : WATER :: BIRD : ?
explanation: A fish moves and lives in water, while a bird flies and lives in the sky — the relation is creature to its natural medium.
trick: A nest is where a bird rests, not the medium it lives and moves in — the sky matches water.

statement: AUTHOR : BOOK :: ARCHITECT : ?
explanation: An author creates a book, and an architect creates (designs) a building — the relation is creator to creation.
trick: 'Design' is the architect's action, not the creation itself — the creation is the building.

statement: THERMOMETER : TEMPERATURE :: SPEEDOMETER : ?
explanation: A thermometer measures temperature, and a speedometer measures the speed of a vehicle — instrument to quantity measured.

statement: CANDID : FRANK :: OBSCURE : ?
explanation: Candid and frank are synonyms, so the second pair must also be synonyms: obscure means vague or not clearly expressed.
trick: Decide whether the first pair is synonym, antonym or something else — then mirror it exactly.

statement: OASIS : DESERT :: ISLAND : ?
explanation: An oasis is a fertile, water-bearing area surrounded by desert; an island is a land area surrounded by ocean — a patch of one set within a vast stretch of the other.
trick: Think of the 'surrounded by' relation: small area of relief inside a large expanse.

statement: SYMPHONY : COMPOSER :: PAINTING : ?
explanation: A symphony is a work created by a composer; a painting is a work created by an artist — creation to its creator, in reverse order.
trick: Note the direction: creation first, creator second — keep the same order in the answer pair.

statement:
Remote work has changed how many companies operate. Instead of travelling to an office every day, employees now connect with their teams through video calls, chat tools and shared documents. Companies benefit because they can hire talented people from anywhere in the world, and they spend less on office space. Employees save the time and money they earlier spent on commuting. However, remote work also brings challenges. Some workers feel lonely without colleagues around them, and new employees may find it harder to learn the company's culture. For this reason, many organisations now follow a hybrid model, in which people work from home on some days and come to the office on others.

According to the passage, how do companies benefit from remote work?
options: They can sell more products in other countries
They can hire talented people from anywhere and spend less on office space
Their employees agree to work longer hours
They no longer need offices at all
explanation: The passage states directly: 'Companies benefit because they can hire talented people from anywhere in the world, and they spend less on office space.'
trick: For direct-detail questions, the answer is usually a near-exact line from the passage — scan for the key words.

statement:
Urban trees do much more than decorate our streets. A single large tree can absorb significant amounts of carbon dioxide and release oxygen into the air. Trees also cool their surroundings: shaded areas under trees can be several degrees cooler than nearby open roads, which reduces the need for air-conditioning in summer. Their roots absorb rainwater and reduce flooding during heavy rains. Studies have also shown that people who live near green spaces report lower stress levels. Despite these benefits, trees are often the first victims of road-widening and construction projects. Experts say that protecting existing trees is far cheaper and more effective than planting new saplings, because a mature tree provides benefits that a young plant takes decades to match.

According to the passage, how do trees help during heavy rains?
options: Their leaves stop the rain completely
Their roots absorb rainwater and reduce flooding
They reduce the speed of the wind
They warn people about floods in advance
explanation: The passage states directly: 'Their roots absorb rainwater and reduce flooding during heavy rains.'
